messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos had always taken pride in his work as a prison guard, but that was before his younger brother, Alex, was killed in a senseless act of violence. It had been six months since the funeral, and Carlos still couldn't shake off the feeling of detachment that had settled over him like a shroud. He would find himself zoning out in the middle of conversations, or feeling like he was watching himself go through the motions of his daily routine from outside his body. It started with little things - seeing a news report about another senseless killing, hearing someone talk about losing a loved one, and suddenly Carlos would feel like he was floating above the ground. He'd try to shake off the dissociative feeling by covering his face with his hands, as if physical contact could anchor him back in reality. But it wasn't just the media or conversations that triggered these episodes - anything that reminded him of Alex, from the smell of his cologne to the sound of his favorite song, would send Carlos spiraling. As time went on, Carlos began to notice a pattern: whenever he felt himself starting to detach, he'd pick arguments with his wife or create drama at work. It was as if he needed the adrenaline rush of conflict to distract him from the crushing grief that threatened to overwhelm him. He knew it wasn't healthy, but he couldn't seem to stop himself - and besides, what did it matter? He had no future, no happiness left in his life anyway. The more Carlos struggled with these feelings, the more convinced he became that he was somehow responsible for Alex's death. If only he'd been there, if only he'd been able to protect him... The weight of this self-blame crushed Carlos, making it harder and harder for him to face the world outside his home. He started avoiding anything that reminded him of Alex - photos, mementos, even certain streets they used to walk down together. But avoidance only seemed to make things worse: the more Carlos hid from his grief, the more he felt like he was losing himself. He'd catch glimpses of himself in mirrors or windows and barely recognize the person staring back. And yet, every time he tried to confront these feelings head-on, he'd feel that familiar sense of detachment creeping back in - as if his own mind was conspiring against him. Carlos's wife had been patient with him so far, but he could see the strain starting to show on her face. She didn't understand why he couldn't just "get over it" already - after all, hadn't they both lost Alex? But for Carlos, there was no "getting over" this kind of pain. It was as if he'd been sentenced to a life term in his own private prison, with no parole in sight. It was the look on his wife's face that finally brought Carlos to seek help - the same look he saw every time he walked out the door to go to work, feeling like a shadow of the man he used to be. He didn't know what he hoped for from therapy, but he knew he couldn't keep living like this. The thought of facing his grief head-on was terrifying, but it was also the only way Carlos could see to start rebuilding himself - and maybe, just maybe, find a way out of the darkness that had consumed him.
